Palantir Technologies, Inc. (PLTR) stock has little room for error at its current valuation, despite the company's strong growth. The Florida-based software platform developer has lost 8% of its market value so far this year, even after delivering standout Q3 results and raising full-year guidance across key financial metrics. Yet following that pullback, shares still trade at a steep forward P/E multiple of 96x.

Although Palantir's rapid top-line expansion justifies a premium valuation, a closer look at total contract value (TCV), the international commercial segment, and the earnings sensitivity to certain macro developments suggests the stock is already priced for perfection. For these reasons, I am Bearish on Palantir.

Slow TCV Growth Raises Questions

One of the main reasons behind my Bearish stance on Palantir is the massive gap between TCV growth and revenue growth. In Q3 2026, TCV grew just 6% year-over-year to $2.92 billion, while revenue surged 96% year-over-year to $2.31 billion. Meanwhile, year-over-year TCV growth decelerated sharply from 49% in Q2 when TCV reached $3.37 billion.

At a fundamental level, the disconnect between revenue growth and TCV growth highlights shorter initial contract durations for new contracts. This contrasts with Palantir's historical operational profile, when the company enjoyed multi-year government contracts. On the Q3 earnings call, CFO David Glazer revealed that several eight-figure contracts were shorter in duration compared to historical averages.

CFO Glazer elaborated that he expects contract durations to eventually increase. "We signed multiple 8-figure deals in the quarter that were shorter in duration than usual, as customers rapidly adopted initial sovereign AI capabilities in their enterprise. It is important to remember that the sovereign AI revolution is only 1 quarter old. As we continue to deliver value with sovereign AI, over time, we expect both the duration and size of these contracts to increase."

From a valuation perspective, the problem with shorter contract durations is that customers reach renewal or renegotiation dates sooner. Strong revenue conversion today does not automatically lock in multi-year cash flows unless Palantir sustains high retention and expands initial terms at renewal. Slow TCV growth, therefore, highlights this risk faced by the company. I believe Palantir's valuation multiples will continue to compress in the next few quarters as the market digests this business transition.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) secured a defense contract reportedly worth around $300 million from Poland on Friday, amid an increasing use of AI in critical defense and military operations.

PLTR shares closed up 5.4%, its fifth straight session of gains and best week in nearly four months. The stock saw its best week since August, according to Koyfin data.

Poland Turns To AI For Military Decision-Making

Under a five-year agreement, Palantir will supply its artificial intelligence-powered Maven Smart System to help the Polish military analyze information, identify threats and make faster decisions.

Poland's defense ministry said the software would operate within the military's own infrastructure, with Palantir having no access to sensitive data, encryption keys or remote access to the system.

"All keys, servers, and information are and will remain in the exclusive possession of the Polish Army. We are purchasing the tool, but the information we will be placing and extracting from it belongs solely to Poland," Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

The ministry added that while AI would assist in assessing threats and risks, final decisions would remain with authorized military personnel.

"We are going to begin significant investment into the Polish ecosystem, both hiring more people and looking for investment opportunities," Palantir CEO Alex Karp said, as quoted by Bloomberg.

MSS Reportedly Helped Strike 1000 Targets With First 24 Hours In Iran War

Maven is an AI-powered platform that uses information from multiple sources, enabling the military to analyze large volumes of data through a single system. The system is also used by NATO.

The U.S. reportedly used the Maven Smart System to help strike more than 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours of the Iran war.

title: 5 Stocks That Should Double in 3 Years
detail:
5 Stocks That Should Double in 3 Years
Habib Ur Rehman

CRWD
ARGX
LLY
TKO
PLTR
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A stock can nearly double in three years without tapping into huge market hype. If investors are still willing to pay a similar price for each dollar of profit at the end, the business can deliver nearly the entire return through earnings growth.

That route sounds simple enough until the sources of growth are pulled apart. Revenue can climb because a company is winning customers, selling more to the ones it already has or raising prices without hurting demand. Profit can grow faster than sales when fixed costs are spread across a larger base. By contrast, a lower tax bill or a burst of cost cutting may lift one year results without laying the foundation for the next two.

The strongest compounding companies usually have more than one engine. For example, a drugmaker can reach a much larger patient population while new manufacturing capacity relieves supply constraints, a commerce platform can add merchants, process more transactions and earn more from each relationship.

Per-share economics is just as important as companywide profit since stock-based compensation can absorb part of the gain before it reaches existing owners, while debt service and heavy capital spending can limit the cash left for reinvestment or buybacks. The debate over whether this AI company's cash flow is staying ahead of dilution is a useful example. A rapidly expanding business still has to turn that success into lasting value for each share.

Valuation is the other half of the equation because if earnings double while the price-to-earnings multiple is cut in half, the stock goes nowhere. A high starting multiple is not automatically fatal, since rapid growth can make today's price look much less demanding in two or three years. A low multiple offers no promise either as it can signal that investors expect the company's best days to fade.

Three years is a long-enough time for operating progress to reshape a company's financial profile, but short enough that a missed product launch, a tougher competitor or slower customer spending can change the outcome. A sharp selloff does not always make a growth stock attractive, just as a strong run does not prove that the opportunity has passed. An e-commerce giant's recovery after investors returned to the beaten-down stock illustrates how quickly expectations can reset when the business improves.

The companies below approach the same destination through very different businesses, including medicines, digital commerce, security, data platforms, cloud services and electrical equipment. None needs a speculative surge in its valuation to produce a double. The central case is that sustained earnings growth can carry most of the return. If execution gets weak or investors assign a much lower multiple, the math turns against shareholders just as quickly.

November has been tough on tech stocks. The Nasdaq Composite slid around 7% from the end of October to Wednesday, Nov. 25, putting the index about 15% below the record close it set on Oct. 6.

Some big growth stocks are down far more. Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) shares, at $59.41 after Wednesday's close, have lost over half their value since their record close in June 2025. Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) trades around 14% under its Aug. 3 record close, and Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) is about 22% off the record close it set on Oct. 9.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

But I think all three are worth considering in December and holding into 2027. Each reported something in its last quarter that its stock price doesn't seem to reflect.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Netflix's members are staying put

Netflix raised prices again this year, including in the U.S. Still, its churn (the share of members who cancel) improved year over year in the third quarter, both worldwide and in the U.S. It was also better than management had predicted.

On the third-quarter earnings call in October, co-CEO Greg Peters called churn "the best evidence that we've got that we're delivering [value to members]."

This matters because much of Netflix's growth comes from raising prices, which tends to work only when members stay. And at around 16 times its expected 2027 earnings, Netflix is the cheapest of the three stocks.

But revenue growth might keep slowing. Third-quarter revenue climbed 11.8%, versus 17.2% growth a year before. And Netflix expects 11.5% for the fourth quarter. If growth keeps falling, the shares might stay cheap for a long time.

2. Amazon: chips it designs itself

Amazon Web Services (AWS), the company's cloud computing unit, grew revenue 39% year over year in the third quarter, its sixth straight quarter of faster growth. One part of AWS is growing even faster: the chips Amazon designs itself.

On the third-quarter earnings call, CEO Andy Jassy said the chips business is growing at "triple digit percentages year over year." He added that revenue commitments for Graviton, Amazon's general-purpose processor, and Trainium, its artificial intelligence (AI) chip, have each risen more than 20-fold in the last year. Customers using Amazon's own chips saved more than $2 billion in the third quarter alone, he said, and Amazon plans to offer Trainium outside AWS in late 2027. On Nov. 23, Amazon also agreed to buy Decart's AI optimization technology and hire the start-up's founders and engineers, who have worked with Amazon on Trainium since 2025.

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) stock jumped 4.5% on the final day of the week, Friday, boosted by news that the tech giant has just won an artificial intelligence defense contract with Poland.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

What Palantir won

Valued at $300 million over five years, the contract pays for software that will "support decision-making processes ​by army commanders," according to Reuters, which reports that Palantir has been cooperating with the Polish ministry of defense since 2025.

That's probably the most important information in this announcement -- how recent Palantir's relationship with Poland is. Even $300 million isn't a lot of money for Palantir, after all, especially when spread over five years. That's only $60 million per year, or barely 0.8% of Palantir's total revenue stream.

But just last year, all Palantir had was a "memorandum of understanding" with Poland. Today, it has a small contract and a relationship that can grow over time.

What's next for Palantir

Polish defense minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz calls this "a watershed ⁠moment for the operational capabilities of ​the Armed Forces of the ​Republic of Poland." I don't know that the moment is quite that significant for Palantir. Still, it will help to maintain the stock's remarkable earnings growth rate, estimated at 62.5% annually over the next five years.

At a valuation of more than 96x free cash flow, and a 106.5 price-to-earnings ratio, I wouldn't call Palantir stock "cheap" -- and that's probably the primary reason Palantir has underperformed the S&P 500 over the past year. But a 62.5% growth rate could change that valuation in a hurry.

If it gets a little cheaper, I might just buy Palantir stock myself.
